property_summary: After calling lockInGuess with exactly 1 ether, the contract records the guess (so settle can later pay out) — i.e., lockInGuess accepts 1 ether and sets a nonzero block for the caller.
lockInGuess accepts and does not revert for 1 ether deposits (i.e., callers sending exactly 1 ether should succeed).
For any deposit amount, lockInGuess succeeds for callers sending exactly 1 ether and fails (reverts) for callers sending any amount different from 1 ether.
For any call to lockInGuess, lockInGuess succeeds (does not revert) iff the attached value equals 1 ether.
lockInGuess reverts exactly when the sent value is not 1 ether (i.e., it succeeds iff the caller sends 1 ether).

For any caller and any guess hash, calling lockInGuess with exactly 1 ether always succeeds on the reference contract (it accepts msg.value == 1 ether) but the mutant that requires 2 ether will reject (revert) for calls sending 1 ether, so there exists inputs where the mutant fails while the reference succeeds.

For any caller and any guess hash, calling lockInGuess with 1 ether when the caller already has a pending guess must be rejected by the reference (it enforces no overwrite) whereas the mutant allows overwriting an existing guess; thus the reference never lets a second lockInGuess call succeed for the same caller without settling first, but the mutant sometimes does.

After any successful lockInGuess call by a player sending exactly 1 ether, the stored Guess.block for that player equals the next block number (block.number + 1) in the reference; the mutant that stores block.number instead will sometimes store a different value and thus violate this rule.

After any successful lockInGuess call sending exactly 1 ether, the reference contract always records guesses(player).block == block.number + 1, while the mutant that stores block.number will make guesses(player).block != block.number + 1 for some inputs (i.e., when lockInGuess is called and observed in the same block).

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess by sending exactly 1 ether, the reference contract always records guesses(caller).block equal to the next block number (block.number + 1) after the call completes; the mutant that stores block.number will sometimes record a different value, so asserting guesses(caller).block == block.number + 1 holds for the reference for all inputs but is falsified by the mutant for some inputs.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess paying exactly 1 ether, the reference C records guesses(caller).block != block.number (it stores block.number+1), whereas the mutant that stores block.number will make guesses(caller).block == block.number for some inputs; thus the invariant guesses(caller).block != block.number holds for the reference for all inputs but is violated by the mutant for some inputs.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess paying exactly 1 ether, the reference C always records guesses(caller).block equal to block.number + 1 (i.e. strictly greater than the current block number), while the mutant that stores block.number can record a stored block equal to the current block number, violating the strict greater-than relation.

For any caller and any guess bytes32, after lockInGuess(...) completes the reference contract C always records the guess in its public mapping before the block pointer is nonzero (i.e., the stored guess equals the provided hash whenever the stored block is nonzero), while the mutant that sets block before guess can transiently leave block nonzero with the old/empty guess and thus violate this invariant for some inputs/attacker behavior.

For any caller and any guess hash, after a successful lockInGuess call the reference contract always has both guesses[caller].block != 0 => guesses[caller].guess == providedHash (i.e., if block is set then guess equals the supplied hash); the mutant that sets block before guess can expose a state where block is nonzero but guess is still the old value when an external call (to a reentrant attacker) observes state, thus violating the rule for some inputs.

Invariant: Immediately after lockInGuess returns, either the stored block for msg.sender is zero, or the stored guess equals the hash passed; the mutant that writes block before guess can transiently leave block != 0 while guess is still the old value by triggering a reentrant call from a malicious contract during lockInGuess, so there exist inputs (a malicious caller contract plus a chosen hash) that make this invariant false for the mutant but it holds for the reference.

For any caller and any hash, if a caller successfully calls lockInGuess (call does not revert) then immediately after the call the stored guesses[caller].guess equals the passed hash; the mutant that sets block before guess can allow a reentrant attacker to observe block nonzero while guess is still the old value causing the stored guess to differ from the supplied hash for some input.

For any caller and any guess hash, after a (non-reverting) lockInGuess call completes on the correct contract, the stored guesses[caller].guess equals the provided hash (i.e., if lockInGuess returns OK then the mapping's guess matches the input); the mutant that writes block before guess can allow a reentrant attacker to observe/leave inconsistent state causing this to fail for some attacker contract and hash.

After a successful lockInGuess call by any address with exactly 1 ether, the stored guess for that address equals the provided hash; the mutant temporarily clears guess causing an intermediate observable zero which can be observed if another caller reads the guess between writes (the reference always leaves guess equal to the provided hash at call completion, the mutant also ends equal but an adversarial reentrant caller can observe the zero during execution), so a reentrant callee can detect the transient zero — the reference prevents any reentrant observation while the mutant exposes it.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess with 1 ether, after the call completes the stored guess for that caller is equal to the supplied hash; the one-statement mutant temporarily clears the guess and can be observed by a reentrant callee during execution, breaking the rule for some inputs (a reentrant attacker address).

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess paying 1 ether, the contract never observes a zero guess for that caller during lockInGuess execution (no reentrant observer can see guess == 0); the mutant briefly clears guess to zero allowing a reentrant attacker to observe guess == 0 during the call.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess paying 1 ether, after the call completes the stored guess for that caller equals the provided hash (the reference preserves this invariant throughout and at completion; the mutant temporarily clears guess allowing a reentrant attacker to observe a zero during execution and thus can break the invariant for some interaction patterns).

For any caller paying exactly 1 ether to lockInGuess, attempting a reentrant call into a view getter during lockInGuess must never observe the stored guess as zero (the reference never exposes a zero guess during execution), whereas the mutant briefly sets guess to zero and a reentrant attacker can observe that zero.

After a successful settle call that may payout, the reference contract always resets guesses[msg.sender].block to 0 (so the stored block number becomes zero), whereas the mutant leaves the stored block number nonzero for some inputs, allowing a difference observable via the public getter.

For any actor who calls lockInGuess and later calls settle, the reference contract always resets their stored guess.block to 0 after settle returns; the mutant that omits this reset will for some fuzzed inputs leave guesses[actor].block non-zero, violating that invariant.

For any actor who successfully lockInGuess and then calls settle after the required block has passed, the reference contract always clears guesses[actor].block to 0 (so the public getter returns 0), whereas the mutant that omits this reset can leave guesses[actor].block non-zero for some inputs.

For any actor who calls lockInGuess and later calls settle after the required block, the reference contract always clears their stored guesses[actor].block to 0; the mutant that omits the reset can leave guesses[actor].block non-zero for some fuzzed inputs, so reading the public getter after settle will differ.

After any actor calls lockInGuess and then calls settle (after advancing block), the correct contract always clears guesses[actor].block to 0; the mutant that omits that reset can leave guesses[actor].block non-zero for some fuzzed inputs, so the public getter guesses(actor).block differs.

After a successful call to settle, the contract resets the caller's stored guess block to zero (so repeated settle calls without a new lockInGuess are no-ops); the mutant that resets the block only after transferring can leave the block non-zero if the transfer to the caller fails, violating that invariant.

For any caller and any locked guess, after settle() finishes the caller's stored guess.block is always cleared (zero) in the correct contract; the mutant that performs the transfer before clearing can leave guess.block non-zero if the transfer to the caller fails.

For any caller who locked a guess, after settle() returns the caller's stored guess.block is always cleared (zero) in the reference; the mutant that does the transfer before clearing can leave guess.block non-zero if the transfer to the caller fails, so using a callee address that reverts on receive will make the mutant preserve a non-zero block while the reference always clears it.

For any caller who locked a guess and then calls settle(), the correct contract always clears their stored Guess.block to zero when settle() finishes; the mutant that moves the clear after the transfer can leave Guess.block non-zero if the transfer to the caller fails (e.g., caller is a reverting receiver).

For any caller who successfully locked a guess, after calling settle() the reference contract always clears guesses[caller].block to 0 (so address(c).balance decreases by 2 ether only when transfer succeeds), whereas the mutant that moves the block reset after the transfer can leave guesses[caller].block non-zero when the transfer to the caller fails (e.g., when the recipient reverts).

For any addr and guess hash, if a player locks in a guess with 1 ETH and then calls settle after the target block, the reference contract only pays out when the stored guess equals the computed answer (so address(c).balance decreases by 2 ether on match only); the mutant inverts that and pays out when the guess != answer, so there exist inputs where the balance change differs.

For any address that previously locked a guess, calling settle will reset that address's stored guess.block to 0 (and may pay out) in the reference; the mutant that uses blockhash(block.number) can cause settle to behave differently because it computes the answer from the current block rather than the stored block, making the stored block clearing or payout outcome differ for some inputs.

For any caller who previously locked in a guess for block B, calling settle after block B always clears their stored guess.block to 0 in the correct contract; the mutant that computes answer from block.number can in some cases leave guess.block nonzero or otherwise change observable settle outcome, so the invariant 'after settle returns, guesses(caller).block == 0' holds for reference but is violated by the mutant for some inputs.

For any caller who previously locked a guess and then calls settle after the locked block has passed, the reference contract always clears that caller's stored guess.block to 0 (so address(c).balance only decreases when the caller is paid); the mutant that uses blockhash(block.number) can make the settle call revert (due to blockhash of current block returning zero for the immediate block in some EVM contexts) or behave differently so that after calling settle the caller's stored guess.block is not reliably cleared — we assert the invariant that after settle returns successfully the stored guess.block is 0 (reference always holds, mutant is broken for some fuzzed inputs).

For any address that locked a guess and then later calls settle (after the locked block), the reference contract always returns from settle without reverting and clears that caller's stored guess.block (so address(c).balance does not increase unless guess matched); the mutant that uses blockhash(block.number) can cause settle to revert for some inputs (when blockhash(block.number) is zero) which breaks this property.

For any caller who previously locked a guess and then calls settle in a later block, the reference contract always returns from settle (does not revert) and clears the caller's stored guess.block to 0; the mutant that uses blockhash(block.number) can make settle revert (or behave differently) for some inputs, violating this invariant.
